{\bfseries Abstract}\par
\begin{quote}
Unicon historically had no native SSH client: programs that needed remote command execution or file transfer shelled out to an external ssh binary. This report describes the current design and implementation: a client that binds libssh and exposes sessions, multiplexed channels, and SFTP through existing language verbs -- open(), read()/write(), receive(), Attrib(), stat(), remove(), and rename() -- rather than a parallel SSH-specific API. The report covers the connection and channel model, authentication and attributes, examples and use cases, the three I/O tiers, interactive shells, SFTP, build integration, and remaining work.
\end{quote}

\section{1. Introduction}
\label{utr26-sec-intro}

This report describes the current design and implementation of native SSH in the Unicon runtime: how a session is opened, how additional channels and SFTP handles are derived from it, how stream I/O, ordered events, and metadata operations are exposed, and what remains out of scope. It is formatted as a Unicon Technical Report [1]. The language-facing reference lives in \emph{Programming with Unicon} (Chapter 6, "Secure Shell") and the language reference (\texttt{open} mode \texttt{h}, \texttt{Attrib}, \texttt{receive}, \texttt{stat} / \texttt{remove} / \texttt{rename}). \hyperref[utr27-sec-examples]{section 6} collects examples by mode and use case. Automated tests live in \texttt{tests/posix/ssh.icn}.


The feature is optional. A build with libssh present reports \texttt{secure~shell} in \texttt{\&features} (the \texttt{\_SSH} feature flag). Without the library, mode \texttt{h} is ignored and the SSH paths are compiled out, as with other optional features.

\section{2. Motivation and prior art}
\label{utr26-sec-motivation}

Unicon programs that needed SSH previously relied on \texttt{popen()} or pipes to an external \texttt{ssh} process. That is not portable (Windows often has no OpenSSH client in \texttt{PATH}) and gives the program no structured access to channels, exit status, or SFTP. Native primitives let an application authenticate to hosts, run commands, and transfer files without an external process.

\subsection{2.1 Library choice}
\label{utr26-sec-prior}

Two C libraries were considered. \textbf{libssh} (LGPL) supports both client and server, modern key exchange and host keys, and true non-blocking I/O via \texttt{poll(2)}. \textbf{libssh2} (BSD) is client-only and cannot be used fully non-blocking. The implementation binds \textbf{libssh} [2], for server-side optionality later and for the callback API that preserves stdout/stderr arrival order (\hyperref[utr26-sec-receive]{section 8.3}).


A full protocol reimplementation (Paramiko, Go's \texttt{x/crypto/ssh}) would mean owning crypto primitives and protocol-drift / CVE tracking indefinitely. Binding to libssh via the existing C runtime avoids that.

\subsection{2.2 Open as the verb}
\label{utr26-sec-prior-api}

Python (Paramiko) and Go (\texttt{x/crypto/ssh}) both treat "new session" as sugar over "open another channel on this connection." The verb is \textbf{open}, applied to an existing connection object, not "clone" or "duplicate." Unicon already has \texttt{open()} as the universal constructor for files, sockets, SSL, and messaging connections. \texttt{Clone()} is the Graphics-facility naming convention; a distinct \texttt{channel()} function would add a new global name for an operation \texttt{open()} already expresses.

\subsection{2.3 Why not Messaging}
\label{utr26-sec-messaging}

The Messaging facility (HTTP/POP/SMTP, \texttt{rmsg.r}, libtp) [3] is not a fit. Messaging's transport-discipline abstraction has the same 1:1 single-stream limitation as SSL -- no channel-multiplexing concept -- so moving into that world would not solve the multiplexed-channel requirement, only relocate it. SSH's request/channel model (\texttt{exec} / \texttt{shell} / \texttt{sftp} as concurrent channels) also does not map onto Messaging's request/response verb model (\texttt{GET} / \texttt{POST} / \texttt{RETR}). SSH does not route through \texttt{ssh://} URIs or \texttt{Mopen()}. It uses the \texttt{h} mode character and plain \texttt{user@host} string parsing, independent of the Messaging/URI subsystem.

\section{3. Architectural grounding}
\label{utr26-sec-arch}

The implementation follows established SSL and socket patterns rather than inventing a parallel subsystem.


\texttt{union~f} in \texttt{src/h/rstructs.h} is the file block's descriptor slot: a tagged union of \texttt{FILE~*}, socket \texttt{fd}, \texttt{SSL~*} when \texttt{HAVE\_LIBSSL}, and so on, discriminated by status bits at runtime. SSH does \textbf{not} embed libssh objects directly in the union. It adds a pointer, \texttt{struct~SSHfile~*sshf}, matching the Messaging \texttt{MFile~*} precedent. \texttt{SSHfile} is allocated with \texttt{malloc} so pointers to it are stable across garbage collection, and is freed by the close hook, never by the collector. A malloc'd block is required once the session must hold a list of child channels whose addresses survive compaction (\hyperref[utr26-sec-close]{section 10.2}).


Status bits live in \texttt{src/h/rmacros.h}. \texttt{Fs\_Encrypt} is \texttt{0200000000}; SSH takes the next bit, \texttt{Fs\_SSH~=~0400000000}. \texttt{open()}'s mode string is scanned character-by-character in \texttt{src/runtime/fsys.r}. \texttt{e} sets \texttt{Fs\_Encrypt}. SSH uses \texttt{h} / \texttt{H} (\texttt{s} is already the Messaging short-request flag).


Attributes are \texttt{"key=value"} strings passed as trailing arguments to \texttt{open()}, parsed in \texttt{create\_ssh\_session()} the same way \texttt{create\_ssl\_context()} parses SSL attributes -- not a fixed argument list. A leading integer, when present, is a connect timeout in milliseconds, as for plain sockets.


All stream I/O funnels through one dispatch point: \texttt{u\_read()} / \texttt{u\_write()} in \texttt{src/runtime/rposix.r}, which already branch on \texttt{Fs\_Socket} / \texttt{Fs\_Encrypt}. SSH adds a third branch for \texttt{Fs\_SSH}, reading from the arrival-order queue (\hyperref[utr29-sec-io]{section 8}) or \texttt{sftp\_read()}, and writing via \texttt{ssh\_channel\_write()} or \texttt{sftp\_write()}. Nothing above this dispatch (\texttt{reads()}, \texttt{read()}, and so on) needs its own SSH case, except where a line-oriented helper must not wait for a newline that will never arrive (\hyperref[utr26-sec-partial]{section 9.2}).


Close is \textbf{explicit, not GC-driven}. The close hook in \texttt{fsys.r} frees SSL resources directly; there is no finalizer during garbage collection. SSH files follow the same convention -- leaking a channel or session means not calling \texttt{close()}, the same as any other file.


\texttt{receive()} already returns a general-purpose \texttt{posix\_message} record (fields \texttt{addr} and \texttt{msg}) for UDP and raw datagrams. SSH reuses that type for an ordered stdout/stderr/exit-status event stream (\hyperref[utr26-sec-receive]{section 8.3}).


\texttt{stat(f)} already \texttt{type\_case}s on its argument (string path versus open file). SFTP extends both branches (\hyperref[utr26-sec-sftp-meta]{section 11.3}). \texttt{remove()} and \texttt{rename()} gain an optional leading session argument, matching the existing Unicon idiom that many functions take an optional leading file or window (\texttt{write("hello")} versus \texttt{write(f,~"hello")}).

\section{4. Connection and channel model}
\label{utr26-sec-connect}
\subsection{4.1 \texttt{open()} dispatch}
\label{utr26-sec-open}

Two shapes, both using the existing \texttt{open()}. The second argument is the usual mode string; \texttt{h} is a new character in that scan, and \texttt{c} / \texttt{s} after \texttt{h} select a channel or SFTP the same way \texttt{u} after \texttt{n} selects UDP (\texttt{n} is TCP, \texttt{nu} is UDP).

\begin{itemize}
\item 
\texttt{open(host\_or\_"user@host",~"h...",~attrs...)} -- first argument is a string: opens a new authenticated SSH \textbf{session} and, by default, an interactive shell channel on it (\hyperref[utr26-sec-default]{section 4.3}).
\item 
\texttt{open(s,~"hc"/"hs",~attrs...)} -- first argument is an existing SSH session or channel file: opens a \textbf{new channel} (\texttt{hc}) or SFTP handle (\texttt{hs}) on the same underlying session (reusing the transport and authentication, no new handshake). Opening on a channel opens a \textbf{sibling} on the session owner, not a child of the channel.
\end{itemize}

A session opened with \texttt{channel=no} has no channel of its own (\texttt{Fs\_SSH} alone, no \texttt{Fs\_Socket}). It exists so later \texttt{open(s,~"hc")} / \texttt{open(s,~"hs")} calls have an authenticated transport. \texttt{channel=yes} is the default. Combining \texttt{channel=no} with mode \texttt{hc} or \texttt{cmd=} is contradictory and fails with a bad-attribute error.

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
s := open("jafar@" || host, "h", "key=" || keypath)
write(s, "show version\\n")
while line := reads(s) do write(line)
close(s)

s := open("user@host", "h", "key=id_ed25519", "channel=no")
c1 := open(s, "hc", "cmd=uname -a")
c2 := open(s, "hc", "cmd=uptime")
\end{Verbatim}

\subsection{4.2 Host string}
\label{utr26-sec-host}

The first argument is \texttt{host}, \texttt{user@host}, or either with \texttt{:port}. The port uses the same \texttt{host:port} form as socket \texttt{open()}; IPv6 uses \texttt{[addr]:port}. A bare IPv6 literal is not misparsed: an unbracketed host is split on \texttt{:} only when there is a single colon. There is no \texttt{port=} attribute.


\texttt{user@host} wins over a \texttt{user=} attribute. If neither is given, libssh's default user (the local login name) is used.


\texttt{ssh://user@host} URI syntax is not used (\hyperref[utr26-sec-messaging]{section 2.3}).

\subsection{4.3 Default channel: shell, not bare session}
\label{utr26-sec-default}

\texttt{open(host,~"h",~...)} with no \texttt{cmd=} and without \texttt{channel=no} opens a shell on a remote PTY immediately, so the common interactive case is one handle. The PTY is requested with \texttt{TERM} (from \texttt{term=}, else \texttt{\$TERM}, else \texttt{xterm}) and a window size (from \texttt{cols=} / \texttt{rows=}, else the local tty via \texttt{TIOCGWINSZ}, else 80x24). Without a real size, remote \texttt{ls(1)} and friends fall back to one column.


A shell channel has no clean command boundaries: prompt text, echoed input, and output all interleave. For scripted use, prefer mode \texttt{hc} with \texttt{cmd=}, which has clean stdout and a real exit status:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
c := open(s, "hc", "cmd=show version")
\end{Verbatim}

\section{5. Attributes and authentication}
\label{utr26-sec-attrs}

Trailing \texttt{open()} arguments are \texttt{name=value} strings. Empty values and unknown names fail (error 1321). Boolean-style attributes without a value are not accepted -- every attribute must contain \texttt{=}. SFTP is selected by mode character \texttt{s} after \texttt{h} (\texttt{"hs"}), not by a valueless attribute.

\begin{longtable}{lll}
\hline
Attribute & Meaning & Notes \\
\hline
\endfirsthead
\hline
Attribute & Meaning & Notes \\
\hline
\endhead
\hline
\endfoot
\hline
\endlastfoot
\texttt{user=} & Remote login name & Overridden by \texttt{user@host} \\
\texttt{key=} & Path to a private key file & Same convention as SSL's \texttt{key=} \\
\texttt{keypass=} & Passphrase for an encrypted private key & Same name as TLS/crypto; distinct from SSH \texttt{password=} \\
\texttt{password=} & Remote login password & Not a TLS attribute; crypto still accepts it as an alias for \texttt{keypass=} \\
\texttt{verifyPeer=} & \texttt{yes} (default) or \texttt{no} & Same spelling as TLS; overrides mode \texttt{-} \\
\texttt{hostkeyfile=} & Path to an OpenSSH \texttt{known\_hosts} file & Passed to libssh as \texttt{SSH\_OPTIONS\_KNOWNHOSTS} \\
\texttt{cmd=} & Command for a one-shot exec channel & Requires mode \texttt{hc}; contradicts \texttt{channel=no} \\
\texttt{channel=} & \texttt{yes} (default) or \texttt{no} & \texttt{no} is transport-only \\
\texttt{term=} & Remote \texttt{TERM} for a PTY & Default \texttt{\$TERM} or \texttt{xterm} \\
\texttt{cols=} / \texttt{rows=} & PTY size & Default from the local tty, else 80x24 \\
\end{longtable}


\texttt{keypass=} is the shared name for a key-file passphrase on TLS, crypto, and SSH. SSH \texttt{password=} remains the remote login password and is not accepted on TLS. Crypto still accepts \texttt{password=} as an alias for \texttt{keypass=}.


The \texttt{-} mode-character flag disables peer verification on TLS (\texttt{ne-}) and SSH (\texttt{h-}), the same as \texttt{verifyPeer=no}. An explicit \texttt{verifyPeer=} overrides the mode flag. \texttt{Fs\_Encrypt} and \texttt{Fs\_SSH} are mutually exclusive contexts, so there is no conflict.


A leading integer attribute is a connect timeout in milliseconds and is applied as libssh's \texttt{SSH\_OPTIONS\_TIMEOUT} / \texttt{TIMEOUT\_USEC}. The default port is 22 when \texttt{:port} is omitted.

\subsection{5.1 Authentication order}
\label{utr26-sec-auth}

If both \texttt{key=} and \texttt{password=} are given, they are tried in the order the attributes appear in the call, not in a hardcoded priority. If \textbf{neither} is given, the implementation falls back to \texttt{ssh\_userauth\_publickey\_auto()} -- default identities under \texttt{\textasciitilde{}/.ssh} and a running agent -- not to password authentication. Agent use through this fallback is supported; an explicit \texttt{agent=} attribute and keyboard-interactive auth remain out of scope.


\texttt{key=} does not expand \texttt{\textasciitilde{}}. Callers (and the \texttt{ussh} demo) must expand a leading \texttt{\textasciitilde{}/} themselves; libssh treats the path literally.

\section{6. Examples and use cases}
\label{utr26-sec-examples}

These examples assume a Unicon build with the \texttt{secure~shell} feature. Connection failures fail with \texttt{\&errortext} set; the usual form is \texttt{s~:=~open(...)~|~stop(\&errortext)}. The packaged demo \texttt{uni/progs/ussh.icn} is a small client that covers the interactive and one-shot command cases.

\subsection{6.1 Modes}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-modes}

Like every other \texttt{open()}, SSH uses the second argument as a mode string (it defaults to \texttt{"r"} when omitted, which is not useful for SSH). \texttt{h} / \texttt{H} is a mode character in that same scan, alongside \texttt{r} / \texttt{w} / \texttt{n} / \texttt{e} / \texttt{m}. After \texttt{h}, \texttt{c} selects a command/channel and \texttt{s} selects SFTP -- the same "facility letter, then modifier" order as \texttt{nu} (UDP) and \texttt{ms} (Messaging short-request). \texttt{n} alone is TCP. Without a preceding \texttt{h}, \texttt{c} is still create+write and \texttt{s} is still ignored (or Messaging short-request after \texttt{m}). Trailing \texttt{"name=value"} arguments are attributes, not modes -- the same slot SSL uses for \texttt{key=} and friends.


Mode characters combine. \texttt{"h-"} is SSH plus skip host-key verification (the \texttt{-} flag also disables SSL peer checks). \texttt{"hc"} is a channel (exec when \texttt{cmd=} is given, else a shell). \texttt{"hs"} is SFTP; \texttt{r} / \texttt{w} / \texttt{a} / \texttt{b} set transfer intent (\texttt{"hsw"}, or \texttt{open(...,~"hs",~...,~"w")}).

\begin{longtable}{lll}
\hline
Form & Kind & Handle \\
\hline
\endfirsthead
\hline
Form & Kind & Handle \\
\hline
\endhead
\hline
\endfoot
\hline
\endlastfoot
\texttt{open(host,~"h",~...)} & mode \texttt{h} & New session plus a PTY shell \\
\texttt{open(host,~"h-",~...)} & mode \texttt{h} and \texttt{-} & Same, no host-key check \\
\texttt{open(host,~"hc",~"cmd=...")} & mode \texttt{hc}, attribute \texttt{cmd=} & New session plus an exec channel \\
\texttt{open(host,~"h",~"channel=no")} & mode \texttt{h}, attribute \texttt{channel=} & Session only (no channel) \\
\texttt{open(s,~"hc")} & mode \texttt{hc} on an existing SSH file & Extra shell channel on that session \\
\texttt{open(s,~"hc",~"cmd=...")} & mode \texttt{hc}, attribute \texttt{cmd=} & Extra exec channel on that session \\
\texttt{open(s,~"hs",~"path=...",~"w")} & mode \texttt{hs} plus access chars & SFTP file or directory \\
\texttt{open(host,~"hs",~"path=...",~"w")} & mode \texttt{hs} on a host string & New session plus SFTP (one handle) \\
leading integer & attribute (timeout) & Connect timeout in milliseconds \\
\end{longtable}


\texttt{channel=no} with \texttt{hc} or \texttt{cmd=} fails (error 1321). \texttt{cmd=} without \texttt{c} also fails.

\subsection{6.2 Interactive shell}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-shell}

With no \texttt{cmd=}, \texttt{open(...,~"h")} requests a remote PTY and shell. \texttt{net::ssh\_interactive(s)} attaches the local tty (raw mode, \texttt{select()} with \texttt{\&input}, CRLF for display):

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
import net

procedure main()
   s := open("user@host", "h", "key=/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519") |
        stop(&errortext)
   ssh_interactive(s)
   close(s)
end
\end{Verbatim}


\texttt{term=}, \texttt{cols=}, and \texttt{rows=} override the PTY. Mode \texttt{"h-"} skips \texttt{known\_hosts} (useful on a first connect before the key is installed). Password auth uses \texttt{password=} instead of, or in addition to, \texttt{key=}.

\subsection{6.3 Remote command}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-cmd}

Mode \texttt{"hc"} with \texttt{cmd=} runs one command and returns its stdout through ordinary \texttt{read()} / \texttt{reads()}. \texttt{Attrib(c,~"exitstatus")} is the remote exit code once it has arrived:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
procedure main()
   s := open("user@host", "hc", "key=/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519",
             "cmd=uname -a") | stop(&errortext)
   while write(read(s))
   write("exit status: ", Attrib(s, "exitstatus"))
   close(s)
end
\end{Verbatim}


The host string may include a port (\texttt{user@host:2222}) or an IPv6 address (\texttt{user@[2001:db8::1]:22}). A leading integer is a connect timeout in milliseconds:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
s := open("user@host", "hc", 5000, "cmd=true") | stop(&errortext)
\end{Verbatim}

\subsection{6.4 Ordered stdout and stderr}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-receive}

Stream \texttt{reads()} see stdout only. When stdout and stderr must stay in arrival order, or when stderr should go to \texttt{\&errout}, use \texttt{receive()}:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
s := open("user@host", "hc", "key=/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519",
          "cmd=echo out; echo err 1>&2; exit 3") | stop(&errortext)
while m := receive(s) do
   case m.addr of \{
      "stdout" : writes(&output, m.msg)
      "stderr" : writes(&errout, m.msg)
      "exit"   : write(&errout, "[exit ", trim(m.msg), "]")
      \}
close(s)
\end{Verbatim}


\texttt{Attrib(c,~"stderr")} is the other stderr path: it drains bytes accumulated since the previous call, without preserving order against stdout. See \hyperref[utr29-sec-io]{section 8}.

\subsection{6.5 Several channels on one session}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-channels}

\texttt{channel=no} opens an authenticated transport. Later \texttt{open(s,~"hc")} / \texttt{open(s,~"hs")} calls add exec, shell, or SFTP handles on that session. Closing \texttt{s} invalidates every derived handle:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
s := open("user@host", "h", "key=/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519",
          "channel=no") | stop(&errortext)
c1 := open(s, "hc", "cmd=uname -a") | stop(&errortext)
c2 := open(s, "hc", "cmd=uptime") | stop(&errortext)
while write(read(c1))
while write(read(c2))
close(c1)
close(c2)
close(s)
\end{Verbatim}


Opening on an existing channel opens a sibling on the session owner, not a child of that channel.

\subsection{6.6 SFTP}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-sftp}

The same session carries SFTP. Mode \texttt{"hs"} plus \texttt{path=} opens a remote file or, if the path is a directory, lists it. \texttt{stat}, \texttt{remove}, and \texttt{rename} take the session as a leading argument:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
s := open("user@host", "h", "key=/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519",
          "channel=no") | stop(&errortext)

c := open(s, "hs", "path=/tmp/out.bin", "w") | stop(&errortext)
writes(c, ReadBytes("local.bin"))
close(c)

info := stat(s, "/tmp/out.bin") | stop(&errortext)
write("remote size: ", info.size)

d := open(s, "hs", "path=/tmp") | stop(&errortext)
while write(read(d))
close(d)

rename(s, "/tmp/out.bin", "/tmp/out.bin.bak")
remove(s, "/tmp/out.bin.bak")
close(s)
\end{Verbatim}

\subsection{6.7 Concurrent hosts}
\label{utr26-sec-ex-threads}

Each connection is blocking. Concurrent hosts use Unicon \texttt{thread}, one thread per in-flight session:

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
procedure run_cmd(host, key)
   local s, line
   s := open(host, "hc", "key=" || key, "cmd=uname -a") | \{
      write(&errout, host, ": ", &errortext)
      fail
      \}
   while line := read(s) do write(host, ": ", line)
   close(s)
end

procedure main()
   local host, key
   key := "/home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519"
   every host := "user@alpha" | "user@beta" | "user@gamma" do
      thread run_cmd(host, key)
end
\end{Verbatim}


Channels that share a session serialize on the session mutex (\hyperref[utr26-sec-mutex]{section 10.1}). Separate sessions do not.

\section{7. Error handling}
\label{utr26-sec-errors}

Connection and channel failures \textbf{fail}, they do not \texttt{runerr}. This matches the SSL connect path: set \texttt{\&errortext}, tear down what was allocated, and fail, so callers write \texttt{if~s~:=~open(...)~then~...~else~...}. Runtime errors are reserved for type mistakes (passing a non-SSH file to \texttt{open(s,~"hc")}, a bad \texttt{Attrib} name on an SSH file).


Error numbers, defined in \texttt{src/runtime/data.r}:

\begin{longtable}{lll}
\hline
Number & Text & Typical cause \\
\hline
\endfirsthead
\hline
Number & Text & Typical cause \\
\hline
\endhead
\hline
\endfoot
\hline
\endlastfoot
1320 & SSH error & Connect failure, allocation, bad host string \\
1321 & bad ssh attribute & Unknown name, empty value, \texttt{cmd=} without \texttt{c}, \texttt{channel=no} with \texttt{hc} \\
1322 & SSH authentication error & No method succeeded \\
1323 & SSH host key verification error & Server not in \texttt{known\_hosts} (when verifying) \\
1324 & SSH channel error & Channel open, I/O, or a closed/cascaded handle \\
1325 & SFTP error & SFTP subsystem, path, or transfer failure \\
\end{longtable}


\texttt{set\_ssh\_errortext()} appends libssh's own message where available. Blocking libssh calls run under \texttt{DEC\_NARTHREADS}; \texttt{\&errortext} is set only after the thread is re-registered, because Unicon allocation is not allowed while unregistered.

\section{8. I/O: streams, \texttt{Attrib()}, and \texttt{receive()}}
\label{utr26-sec-io}

Three tiers, layered simple-default to full-fidelity. All three share one per-channel event queue populated by libssh callbacks (\hyperref[utr26-sec-queue]{section 8.4}).

\subsection{8.1 Plain stream I/O}
\label{utr26-sec-stream}

\texttt{read()} / \texttt{write()} / \texttt{reads()} / \texttt{writes()} work unmodified via the existing \texttt{u\_read()} / \texttt{u\_write()} dispatch, extended with an \texttt{Fs\_SSH} branch. Stream reads consume \textbf{stdout only}. They are enough when the caller does not need to distinguish stderr or preserve cross-stream order.


Writes to a channel call \texttt{ssh\_channel\_write()} and retry short writes. Writes to a transport-only session (no channel) fail with

\begin{enumerate}
\item 
SFTP regular files use \texttt{sftp\_write()} on the same path.
\end{enumerate}
\subsection{8.2 \texttt{Attrib()} for exit status, stderr, and EOF}
\label{utr26-sec-attrib}

\texttt{Attrib()} already exists generically -- documented as "read/write attributes (threads, sockets, ...)" -- and is already used for socket options. SSH channels add three query-only names:

\begin{itemize}
\item 
\texttt{Attrib(c,~"exitstatus")} -- the remote command's exit status, as an integer. \textbf{Fails until the exit-status callback has fired.} The implementation pumps the channel until that happens or the channel is done with no status. Preferring callback state over libssh's blocking \texttt{get\_exit\_*} helpers avoids version-sensitive fallbacks once callbacks are registered. This reuses the ordinary Unicon "fail = not ready" idiom, the same as \texttt{read()} failing at EOF.
\item 
\texttt{Attrib(c,~"stderr")} -- drains \textbf{only new bytes since the last call} (a live incremental accessor, not a cumulative snapshot). Not gated on EOF: reading partial stderr mid-run is safe and useful. Returns a possibly empty string.
\item 
\texttt{Attrib(c,~"eof")} -- \texttt{1} once the remote sent EOF, else \texttt{0}. Useful when a caller is multiplexing with \texttt{select()} and needs to distinguish "no stdout yet" from "channel finished."
\end{itemize}

Unknown names on an SSH file raise 1321.

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
c := open(s, "hc", "cmd=apply-config /tmp/newconfig.json")
while line := reads(c) do process(line)
if \\Attrib(c, "exitstatus") = 0 then write("ok")
else write("failed: " || Attrib(c, "stderr"))
\end{Verbatim}

\subsection{8.3 \texttt{receive()} for ordered events}
\label{utr26-sec-receive}

A command can produce interleaved stdout and stderr where the caller needs to know \emph{when} an stderr message occurred relative to stdout. Neither \texttt{reads()} (stdout only) nor \texttt{Attrib(c,~"stderr")} (a separate drain) can preserve that.


\texttt{receive(c)} on an SSH channel yields the next queued event as a \texttt{posix\_message} whose \texttt{addr} is \texttt{"stdout"}, \texttt{"stderr"}, or \texttt{"exit"} and whose \texttt{msg} is the payload. The exit status is kept as a \textbf{string} so \texttt{receive()}'s return type stays uniform across every kind of file it can be called on; Unicon's \texttt{=} already coerces numeric strings.

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
c := open(s, "hc", "cmd=process_records")
while m := receive(c) do
   case m.addr of \{
      "stdout" : write("OUT: " || m.msg)
      "stderr" : write("ERR: " || m.msg)
      "exit"   : write("done, status " || m.msg)
      \}
\end{Verbatim}


\texttt{receive()} fails once the channel is exhausted.

\subsection{8.4 Arrival-order queue}
\label{utr26-sec-queue}

Preserving cross-stream order requires libssh's \textbf{callback API} (\texttt{ssh\_channel\_callbacks}, with a \texttt{channel\_data\_function} receiving an \texttt{is\_stderr} flag) -- not \texttt{ssh\_channel\_poll()} / \texttt{ssh\_channel\_read()}, which buffer stdout and stderr separately and lose interleaving. Callbacks are registered \textbf{before} the channel is opened so early data cannot land in libssh's own buffers.


Each callback appends a tagged chunk (\texttt{SSH\_CHUNK\_STDOUT} / \texttt{STDERR} / \texttt{EXIT}) to a heap-allocated linked list on the \texttt{SSHfile}. Callbacks can fire inside blocking libssh calls made while the thread is unregistered (\texttt{DEC\_NARTHREADS}), where Unicon allocation is not allowed. \texttt{ssh\_pump()} drives \texttt{ssh\_channel\_poll\_timeout()} so the callbacks run. Stream reads consume stdout chunks; \texttt{Attrib(c,~"stderr")} drains stderr chunks; \texttt{receive()} pops whatever is at the head. One mechanism, three accessors.

\section{9. Interactive shells and \texttt{select()}}
\label{utr26-sec-interactive}
\subsection{9.1 Remote PTY}
\label{utr26-sec-pty}

An interactive channel requests a PTY before \texttt{shell}. Size and \texttt{TERM} are described in \hyperref[utr26-sec-default]{section 4.3}. The session file is also marked \texttt{Fs\_Socket} so existing socket dispatch (including \texttt{select()} and \texttt{get\_fd()}) applies.

\subsection{9.2 Partial-line \texttt{reads()}}
\label{utr26-sec-partial}

Interactive prompts have no trailing newline. The original socket line helper (\texttt{sock\_getstrg}) waits for \texttt{\textbackslash{}n} and hung on a banner or prompt. SSH therefore has its own \texttt{ssh\_getstrg()}: it reads stdout bytes from the queue and returns a partial line at EOF or when the caller's buffer fills, without blocking for a newline that will never come. A seen-but- unconsumed newline is remembered in \texttt{nl\_pending} (libssh has no \texttt{MSG\_PEEK}). \texttt{reads(s,~n)} on a channel is a byte read from the same queue and is the right primitive for an interactive loop.

\subsection{9.3 \texttt{select()} readiness}
\label{utr26-sec-select}

\texttt{select()} on an SSH file must not hang when libssh already buffered the banner during \texttt{open()}. \texttt{ssh\_file\_pending()} nonblocking-pumps the session and reports ready when stdout (or EOF) is queued. Only stdout matters here: stream \texttt{reads()} do not consume stderr/exit chunks, so a nonempty queue of those alone must not make \texttt{select()} claim the file is readable. \texttt{get\_fd()} returns \texttt{ssh\_get\_fd(session)} so the kernel fd participates in the same \texttt{select()} set as ordinary sockets.


On Windows, \texttt{select(\&input)} and \texttt{Attrib(f,~"tty=raw")} / \texttt{"tty=sane"} were added so an interactive client can mux the console with the channel on both Unix and Windows console \texttt{iconx}. Those tty attributes are general (they apply to \texttt{\&input}), not SSH-specific.

\subsection{9.4 \texttt{net::ssh\_interactive()} and \texttt{ussh}}
\label{utr26-sec-helper}

\texttt{uni/lib/ssh.icn} provides \texttt{ssh\_interactive(s)}: put the local tty in raw mode, mux \texttt{\&input} with the remote channel via \texttt{select()}, map lone LF to CRLF when copying remote output to a raw local terminal (needed because raw mode disables \texttt{ONLCR}), and restore the tty before returning. It does not close \texttt{s}. The \texttt{ussh} demo (\texttt{uni/progs/ussh.icn}) is a small OpenSSH-like client built with the other \texttt{uni/progs} demos: interactive shell, or a one-shot remote command via \texttt{receive()}.

\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
s := open("user@host", "h", "key=...") | stop(&errortext)
ssh_interactive(s)
close(s)
\end{Verbatim}

\section{10. Concurrency and channel lifecycle}
\label{utr26-sec-conc}
\subsection{10.1 Shared mutex}
\label{utr26-sec-mutex}

Every \texttt{b\_file} already has a \texttt{mutexid}, and all I/O in \texttt{fsys.r} already locks around it. When a channel is created via \texttt{open(s,~"hc")} / \texttt{open(s,~"hs")}, it does \textbf{not} allocate a fresh mutex id -- it copies the session's existing \texttt{mutexid}. Every channel sharing a session then serializes through the same lock via the existing locking calls in \texttt{u\_read} / \texttt{u\_write} / \texttt{receive} / \texttt{Attrib}. libssh sessions are not safe for uncoordinated concurrent access; two threads each holding a different channel on the same session block each other during actual I/O because they contend for the same mutex.

\subsection{10.2 Child tracking and cascade close}
\label{utr26-sec-close}

A Unicon list of \texttt{b\_file} pointers was considered so the moving collector would relocate them. \texttt{SSHfile} is malloc'd and therefore does not move, so the session owner holds a C linked list of child \texttt{SSHfile~*} (\texttt{children} / \texttt{next} / \texttt{parent}). No Unicon list is required.


\texttt{close(s)} on the session walks that list, force-closes every remaining channel and SFTP handle (same close-hook logic as an explicit \texttt{close()}), marks each child \texttt{closed}, clears its queue, and then disconnects and frees the session. The child's Unicon \texttt{b\_file} stays alive until its own \texttt{close()}, but is unusable immediately -- no dangling libssh objects, no readable leftovers. Closing a channel unlinks it from the owner and frees only that channel.


The SFTP subsystem is created lazily, once, on the session owner (\texttt{ssh\_owner\_sftp()}) and shared by every SFTP file or directory on that session. It is freed when the session closes.

\subsection{10.3 Blocking model}
\label{utr26-sec-block}

I/O uses blocking libssh calls plus Unicon's existing \texttt{thread} mechanism -- one thread per in-flight host or channel. Chosen over non-blocking libssh plus \texttt{select()} as the \emph{primary} model: it requires no partial-read/retry state machines. \texttt{select()} readiness (\hyperref[utr26-sec-select]{section 9.3}) is implemented so interactive muxing works; it is not a full non-blocking I/O API.

\section{11. SFTP}
\label{utr26-sec-sftp}

Three shapes, each mapped onto an existing Unicon pattern.

\subsection{11.1 File transfer -- \texttt{read()} / \texttt{write()}}
\label{utr26-sec-sftp-xfer}
\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
c := open(s, "hs", "path=/tmp/firmware.bin", "w")
while writes(c, ReadBytes(local_fw))
close(c)
\end{Verbatim}


Mode \texttt{"hs"} is SFTP; read/write/append intent comes from the usual mode characters (\texttt{r} / \texttt{w} / \texttt{a} / \texttt{b}), either in the same string (\texttt{"hsw"}) or as a trailing mode-only token. \texttt{path=} is required. Backed by \texttt{sftp\_open()} / \texttt{sftp\_read()} / \texttt{sftp\_write()} / \texttt{sftp\_close()}. Structurally a plain file -- another variant feeding the existing dispatch. SFTP regular files are \textbf{not} marked \texttt{Fs\_Socket}: they are byte streams, not select-able channels.

\subsection{11.2 Directory listing}
\label{utr26-sec-sftp-dir}

Local \texttt{open()} on a path that turns out to be a directory transparently switches to \texttt{opendir()} / \texttt{readdir()}, sets \texttt{Fs\_Directory}, and \texttt{reads()} yields one entry name per call. SFTP does the same: \texttt{open(s,~"hs",~"path=/tmp/configs")} checks the remote path with one \texttt{sftp\_stat()}; if it is a directory, \texttt{sftp\_opendir()} / \texttt{sftp\_readdir()} provide the same \texttt{Fs\_Directory} behavior.

\subsection{11.3 Metadata -- \texttt{stat()}, \texttt{remove()}, \texttt{rename()}}
\label{utr26-sec-sftp-meta}

These extend existing builtins via the leading-optional-file argument idiom, rather than introducing \texttt{sftp\_remove()} names. The signature change is backward-compatible: a string first argument is still the local-filesystem operation.

\begin{itemize}
\item 
\texttt{remove(s,~path)} -- \texttt{sftp\_unlink} when \texttt{s} is an SSH session or channel file.
\item 
\texttt{rename(s,~from,~to)} -- \texttt{sftp\_rename}. \texttt{rename} gained a third argument for this form; \texttt{rename(s1,~s2)} is unchanged.
\item 
\texttt{stat(c)} -- \texttt{sftp\_fstat} on an already-open SFTP file.
\item 
\texttt{stat(s,~path)} -- a single \texttt{sftp\_stat} request, without paying for \texttt{sftp\_open()} + \texttt{sftp\_fstat()}. Both entry points are worth supporting rather than just one.
\end{itemize}
\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small,frame=single,commandchars=\\\{\}]
if info := stat(s, "/tmp/firmware.bin") then
   if info.size = expected_size then pull_it()
\end{Verbatim}


\texttt{sftp2rec()} populates the same \texttt{posix\_stat} record as \texttt{stat2rec()}. SFTP's attribute set is protocol-version dependent; fields the server did not send are left \textbf{null} rather than reported as zero, so callers can tell "absent" from "genuinely zero." SFTP carries atime/mtime, not ctime. Size, uid/gid (name or numeric), permissions-as-mode-string, and file type (\texttt{d} / \texttt{l} / \texttt{c}) are filled when the corresponding flags are present.

\section{12. Build integration}
\label{utr26-sec-build}

\texttt{configure~--disable-ssh} turns the feature off. Otherwise \texttt{CHECK\_LIBSSH} in \texttt{aclocal.m4} probes for \texttt{<libssh/libssh.h>} and \texttt{ssh\_new}, setting \texttt{HAVE\_LIBSSH}. The probe looks under \texttt{/usr/local} (FreeBSD) and \texttt{/opt/homebrew} (macOS) when those prefixes contain the headers, so later compiles do not miss \texttt{libssh/libssh.h}. \texttt{--with-libssh=DIR} overrides the prefix. A required \texttt{--enable-ssh} without the library is a configure error; optional (default) absence degrades gracefully, as with other optional libraries.


\texttt{\&features} reports \texttt{secure~shell} when the library was found. \texttt{tests/posix/Makefile} skips \texttt{ssh} when the feature is absent. CI installs \texttt{libssh-dev} (or the platform equivalent) so the support builds and the deterministic half of the test runs. README install notes list \texttt{libssh-dev} / \texttt{libssh-devel} / \texttt{brew~install~libssh} alongside the other optional libraries.


Guards are \texttt{\#if~HAVE\_LIBSSH} throughout \texttt{rstructs.h}, \texttt{rmacros.h}, \texttt{feature.h}, \texttt{sys.h}, \texttt{fsys.r}, \texttt{rposix.r}, \texttt{fxposix.ri}, and \texttt{fmisc.r}.

\section{13. Status and remaining work}
\label{utr26-sec-status}

\textbf{Keyboard-interactive authentication} and an explicit agent attribute. The \texttt{publickey\_auto} fallback already talks to a running agent.


\textbf{Non-blocking I/O as the primary concurrency model.} \texttt{select()} readiness is implemented; the I/O calls themselves still block. A \texttt{ssh\_set\_blocking(sess,~0)} plus resume state machine is the obvious next step if thread-count pressure appears.


\textbf{SSH server.} libssh can do it; nothing in the runtime exposes it. The mode character and file-status bit leave room, but the accept/listen path is not designed.


\textbf{Default channel type.} Shell-by-default shipped for mode \texttt{"h"}. Scripted use uses \texttt{"hc"} with \texttt{cmd=}. Reconsidering the default remains open and would be a compatibility break.


\textbf{Timeouts.} TCP-connect timeout is the leading integer attribute. There is no separate handshake+auth timeout beyond what that covers, and no exec timeout -- a stuck command blocks until \texttt{close()}, matching ordinary blocking sockets.


\textbf{Trust-on-first-use.} Verification is check-only (\texttt{ssh\_session\_is\_known\_server}). A new host fails with 1323 unless the caller uses \texttt{h-} or installs the key in \texttt{known\_hosts} out of band. The runtime does not write the store.


\textbf{\texttt{\textasciitilde{}} in \texttt{key=}.} Not expanded. The helper and \texttt{ussh} expand \texttt{\textasciitilde{}/} themselves.

\section{Appendix: test coverage}
\label{utr26-sec-coverage}

\texttt{tests/posix/ssh.icn} is deterministic without a server: it checks that \texttt{\&features} reports \texttt{secure~shell}, and that bad attributes, \texttt{channel=maybe}, \texttt{channel=no} combined with \texttt{hc}/\texttt{cmd=}, \texttt{cmd=} without mode \texttt{c}, and a connect to a closed local port all fail with \texttt{\&errortext} set. A live round-trip runs only when \texttt{UNICON\_SSH\_TESTHOST} is set (host or \texttt{user@host}), with optional \texttt{UNICON\_SSH\_TESTPORT}, \texttt{UNICON\_SSH\_TESTKEY}, \texttt{UNICON\_SSH\_KNOWNHOSTS}, and \texttt{UNICON\_SSH\_SFTPPATH}. The live path covers exec stdout, \texttt{Attrib(c,~"exitstatus")}, \texttt{receive()} event tags, partial-line \texttt{reads()} of a \texttt{printf} with no newline, and SFTP write/read/stat/remove of a binary payload.


\texttt{tests/posix/Makefile} skips the test when the feature is absent. Expected default output is \texttt{tests/posix/stand/ssh.std}.
